Indicial polynomials and bb-functions of DD-modules along arbitrary varieties and their computation

Toshinori Oaku
Abstract

We define an indicial polynomial of a DD-module along an arbitrary subvariety as a generalization of both the classical indicial polynomial for a single linear differential equation and the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of a variety defined by Budur-Mustaţã-Saito. An indicial polynomial is also a generalization of the bb-function of a DD-module along a submanifold and can be used in the computation of the DD-module theoretic inverse image by the embedding instead of the bb-function. We consider properties of indicial polynomials and relations with bb-functions. An indicial polynomial may exist even if the bb-function does not, and gives the set of the roots of the bb-function if it exists. Computation of an indicial polynomial is easier than the bb-function and naturally includes the case with parameters.

1 Introduction—Definitions and basic properties

We first define an indicial polyomial of a DD-module along a submanifold as a generalization of the bb-function. This notion can be generalized to an arbitrary subvariety, possibly with singularities and/or multiplicities, by using the technique introduced by Budur, Mustaţã, Saito [2]. This enables us to compute an indicial polynomial and the bb-function of an algebraic DD-module along an arbitrary algebraic set.

Our interest in indicial polynomials comes from the following observations:

  1. 1.

    Compared with bb-functions, indicial polynomials can exist for a broader class of DD-modules which are not necessarily holonomic (see Example 10).

  2. 2.

    An indicial polynomial of a DD-module should give some information on the solutions of the DD-module as in the classical case of a single equation (see, e.g., [21], [12]) if the DD-module has regular singularities along a submanifold YY, at least in case of codimension one.

  3. 3.

    An indicial polynomial can be used for a concrete expression of the DD-module theoretic inverse image by the embedding of a submanifold even if the bb-function does not exist (see Theorems 3, 6, Examples 4, 10).

  4. 4.

    The computation of an indicial polynomial is easier than that of the bb-function and gives the roots of the bb-function if it exists. This serves as a, at least heuristic, method for computing the bb-function with an associated stratification for e.g., holonomic DD-modules, for which the existence of the bb-function is assured (see Example 11).

  5. 5.

    Many important examples of holonomic systems such as AA-hypergeometric systems have parameters. It would be preferable for some purposes to regard parameters as variables. In that case, it should be natural to consider indicial polynomials instead of bb-functions (see Example 12).

In this introduction, we restrict ourselves to the case of submanifold and study general properties of indicial polynomials. Let us first recall definition of the bb-function of a section of a DD-module along a submanifold. Let XX be an nn-dimensional complex manifold and YY a complex analytic submanifold of XX. Let 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X} be the sheaf of holomorphic functions on XX and ℐY{\mathcal{I}}_{Y} be the defining ideal of YY, which is a sheaf of ideals of 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. We denote 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X} the sheaf of (rings of) differential operators on XX with holomorphic coefficients.

The VV-filtration {VYj​(𝒟X)}j∈ℤ\{V^{j}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})\}_{j\in{\mathbb{Z}}} of 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X} along YY is the filtration on the sheaf 𝒟X|Y{\mathcal{D}}_{X}|_{Y}, which is the sheaf-theoretic restriction of 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X} to YY, defined by

VYj(𝒟X):={P∈𝒟X|Y∣PℐYi⊂ℐYi−j(∀i∈ℤ)}V^{j}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X}):=\{P\in{\mathcal{D}}_{X}|_{Y}\mid P{\mathcal{I}}_{Y}^{i}\subset{\mathcal{I}}_{Y}^{i-j}\quad(\forall i\in{\mathbb{Z}})\}

with the convention ℐYj=𝒪X|Y{\mathcal{I}}_{Y}^{j}={\mathcal{O}}_{X}|_{Y} for j≤0j\leq 0. Let θ\theta be a vector field on a neighborhood in XX of each point of YY which induces the identity map on ℐY/ℐY2{\mathcal{I}}_{Y}/{\mathcal{I}}_{Y}^{2}. In local coordinates x=(x1,…,xd,xd+1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{d},x_{d+1},\dots,x_{n}) such that Y={x1=⋯=xd=0}Y=\{x_{1}=\cdots=x_{d}=0\}, we may take

θ=x1​∂∂x1+⋯+xd​∂∂xd.\theta=x_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial{x_{1}}}+\cdots+x_{d}\frac{\partial}{\partial{x_{d}}}.

Note that θ\theta is uniquely determined modulo a vector field which belongs to VY−1​(𝒟X)V_{Y}^{-1}({\mathcal{D}}_{X}).

Definition 1

Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be a coherent left 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module defined on XX. Let uu be a section of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} defined on a neighborhood of p∈Yp\in Y. The bb-function of uu along YY at pp is the monic polynomial b⁡(s)b(s), if any, in an indeterminate ss of the least degree such that

b⁡(θ)​u∈VY−1​(𝒟X)p​ub(\theta)u\in V^{-1}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})_{p}u

holds, that is, there exists a germ PP of ∈VY−1​(𝒟X)\in V^{-1}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X}) at pp such that

(b⁡(θ)+P)​u=0.(b(\theta)+P)u=0.

If there exists such b⁡(s)b(s) for any u∈ℳpu\in{\mathcal{M}}_{p}, then ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is called specializable along YY at pp.

Define an ideal 𝒥Y​(u){\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u) of the sheaf of rings 𝒪Y​[s]{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}[s] on YY by

𝒥Y​(u):={f⁡(s,x′′)∈𝒪Y​[s]∣f⁡(θ,x′′)​u∈VY−1​(𝒟X)​u},{\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u):=\{f(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}[s]\mid f(\theta,x^{\prime\prime})u\in V_{Y}^{-1}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})u\},

where x′′x^{\prime\prime} is a local coordinate system of YY. Then the bb-function at pp is the monic generator of the ideal 𝒥Y​(u)p∩ℂ⁡[s]{\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p}\cap{\mathbb{C}}[s]. The bb-function of a general DD-module was introduced with an existence proof for holonomic DD-modules by Kashiwara and Kawai [7]. See also Laurent [9]. An algorithm to compute the bb-function of a DD-module defined by differential operators with polynomial coefficients along a linear submanifold was given in [17] and [19].

Example 1

Let X=ℂX={\mathbb{C}} and consider the 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module ℳ=𝒟X/𝒟X(x∂x2+(a+bx)∂x){\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{D}}_{X}/{\mathcal{D}}_{X}(x\partial_{x}^{2}+(a+bx)\partial_{x}) with uu the residue class of 1∈𝒟X1\in{\mathcal{D}}_{X} in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Then the bb-function of uu along {0}\{0\} is s⁡(s+a−1)s(s+a-1), where we regard a,b∈ℂa,b\in{\mathbb{C}} as constants.

The bb-function is sometimes called the indicial polynomial in connection with the classical theory of linear ordinary differential equations as in the example above. Here we propose to define the indicial polynomial as a slight generalization of the bb-function.

Definition 2

Let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be a coherent left 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module defined on XX. Let uu be a section of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} defined on a neighborhood of p∈Yp\in Y. Let x′′=(xd+1,…,xn)x^{\prime\prime}=(x_{d+1},\dots,x_{n}) be a local coordinate system of YY around pp. An indicial polynomial of uu along YY at pp is an element b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) of (𝒪Y)p​[s]({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s] with the smallest degree and monic in ss such that b⁡(s,x′′)∈𝒥Y​(u)pb(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in{\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p}, i.e.,

b⁡(θ,x′′)​u∈VY−1​(𝒟X)p​u.b(\theta,x^{\prime\prime})u\in V^{-1}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})_{p}u.

Then there exists a germ PP of ∈VY−1​(𝒟X)\in V^{-1}_{Y}({\mathcal{D}}_{X}) at pp such that

(b⁡(θ,x′′)+P)​u=0.(b(\theta,x^{\prime\prime})+P)u=0.
Example 2

Let X=ℂ2X={\mathbb{C}}^{2} and (x,y)(x,y) be its coordinates. Consider the 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module ℳ=𝒟X/𝒟X(x∂x2+y∂x+∂y2){\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{D}}_{X}/{\mathcal{D}}_{X}(x\partial_{x}^{2}+y\partial_{x}+\partial_{y}^{2}) with uu the residue class of 1∈𝒟X1\in{\mathcal{D}}_{X} in ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Then s⁡(s+y−1)∈(𝒪Y)p​[s]s(s+y-1)\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s] is the indicial polynomial of uu along Y={0}×ℂY=\{0\}\times{\mathbb{C}} at p=(0,y0)p=(0,y_{0}). There is no bb-function of uu along YY at pp.

If d=1d=1, this definition coincides with that of Baouendi-Goulaouic [1] for a single partial differential equation P​u=0Pu=0 which is called Fuchsian along YY. The equation in the above example is Fuchsian along YY. The (multi-valued) analytic solutions around YY of a Fuchsian equation P​u=0Pu=0 are described in terms of the indicial polynomial as was shown by Tahara [21] under some condition on the indicial polynomial, and then by Mandai [12] in full generality.

If d=1d=1, the condition that there exists an indicial polynomial of uu along YY is called ‘elliptic along YY’ by Laurent and Schapira [11]. In case d>1d>1, their ellipticity condition is weaker than the existence of an indicial polynomial. They proved that every cohomology group of the inverse image to YY of a DD-module which is elliptic along YY is coherent over 𝒟Y{\mathcal{D}}_{Y}. Laurent and Monteiro-Fernandes [10] defined Fuchsian DD-modules along YY, which are, roughly speaking, elliptic and regular along YY.

An indicial polynomial coincides with the bb-function if YY is a point. An indicial polynomial is not uniquely determined in general; moreover, it does not necessarily coincide with the bb-function even if ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is holonomic.

Example 3

Consider a system of differential equations

(x∂x−y)u=y2u=0(x\partial_{x}-y)u=y^{2}u=0

on X=ℂ2∋(x,y)X={\mathbb{C}}^{2}\ni(x,y) and let ℳ=𝒟X​u{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{D}}_{X}u be the corresponding 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module. Then ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is holonomic. It is easy to see that s−y+a⁡(y)​y2s-y+a(y)y^{2} is an indicial polynomial of uu along Y={0}×ℂY=\{0\}\times{\mathbb{C}} at (0,0)(0,0) with an arbitrary germ a⁡(y)a(y) of 𝒪Y{\mathcal{O}}_{Y} at 00, while the bb-function of uu along YY at (0,0)(0,0) is s2s^{2}. In fact (x∂x)2u=0(x\partial_{x})^{2}u=0 holds. On the other hand, at (0,y0)(0,y_{0}) with y0≠0y_{0}\neq 0, the indicial polynomial and the bb-function are both 11.

However, we have the following uniqueness.

Proposition 1

In the notation of Definition 2, assume that an indicial polynomial b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) of uu along YY at pp exists. Then

  1. 1.

    b⁡(s,p)∈ℂ⁡[s]b(s,p)\in{\mathbb{C}}[s] is uniquely determined.

  2. 2.

    If f⁡(s,x′′)∈(𝒪Y)p​[s]f(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s] belongs to 𝒥Y​(u)p{\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p}, then f⁡(s,p)f(s,p) is a multiple of b⁡(s,p)b(s,p) in ℂ⁡[s]{\mathbb{C}}[s]. In particular, one has

    𝕍⁡(𝒥Y​(u)|x′′=p):={s∈ℂ∣f⁡(s,p)=0​(∀f⁡(s,x′′)∈𝒥Y​(u)p)}={s∈ℂ∣b⁡(s,p)=0}.{\mathbb{V}}({\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)|_{x^{\prime\prime}=p}):=\{s\in{\mathbb{C}}\mid f(s,p)=0\,(\forall f(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in{\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p})\}=\{s\in{\mathbb{C}}\mid b(s,p)=0\}.

Proof: 1. An indicial polynomial b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) can be written in the form

b⁡(s,x′′)=sm+b1​(x′′)​sm−1+⋯+bm​(x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime})=s^{m}+b_{1}(x^{\prime\prime})s^{m-1}+\cdots+b_{m}(x^{\prime\prime})

with bi​(x′′)∈(𝒪Y)pb_{i}(x^{\prime\prime})\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}. By the definition, b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) is an element of J:=𝒥Y​(u)pJ:={\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p} in this form with the smallest mm.

It suffices to show that if the degree in ss of an element f⁡(s,x′′)f(s,x^{\prime\prime}) of JJ is less than mm then f⁡(s,p)=0f(s,p)=0 holds. Let us prove this claim by induction on m−deg⁡f⁡(s,p)m-\deg f(s,p). Let a⁡(x′′)​sda(x^{\prime\prime})s^{d} be the leading term of f⁡(s,x′′)f(s,x^{\prime\prime}) with respect to ss. If a⁡(p)≠0a(p)\neq 0, then f⁡(s,x)/a⁡(x′′)f(s,x)/a(x^{\prime\prime}) is monic and belongs to JJ. This is a contradiction since d<md<m. Thus we have a⁡(p)=0a(p)=0.

First assume deg⁡f⁡(s,p)=m−1\deg f(s,p)=m-1. Then d=m−1d=m-1 holds and the coefficient of sds^{d} in f⁡(s,p)f(s,p) is a⁡(p)=0a(p)=0. This is a contradiction. Next assume deg⁡f⁡(s,p)=k≤m−2\deg f(s,p)=k\leq m-2. Then

g⁡(s,x′′):=a⁡(x′′)​b​(s,x′′)−sm−d​f​(s,x′′)g(s,x^{\prime\prime}):=a(x^{\prime\prime})b(s,x^{\prime\prime})-s^{m-d}f(s,x^{\prime\prime})

belongs to JJ and is of degree less than mm in ss. Moreover, deg⁡g⁡(s,p)=k+m−d>k\deg g(s,p)=k+m-d>k holds since a⁡(p)=0a(p)=0. By the induction hypothesis g⁡(s,p)=0g(s,p)=0 holds, which implies f⁡(s,p)=0f(s,p)=0.

2. Assume f⁡(s,x′′)f(s,x^{\prime\prime}) belongs to 𝒥Y​(u){\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u). Dividing f⁡(s,x′′)f(s,x^{\prime\prime}) by b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) in (𝒪Y)p​[s]({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s], write

f⁡(s,x′′)=q⁡(s,x′′)​b​(s,x′′)+r⁡(s,x′′)f(s,x^{\prime\prime})=q(s,x^{\prime\prime})b(s,x^{\prime\prime})+r(s,x^{\prime\prime})

Here is a general relation between the bb-function and an indicial polynomial.

Proposition 2

Assume that the bb-funtion b⁡(s)b(s) of uu along YY at p∈Yp\in Y exists. Then

  1. 1.

    An indicial polynomial b~​(s,x′′)\tilde{b}(s,x^{\prime\prime}) of uu along YY at pp exists and b~​(s,p)\tilde{b}(s,p) divides b⁡(s)b(s) in ℂ⁡[s]{\mathbb{C}}[s].

  2. 2.

    The set of the zeros of b~​(s,p)\tilde{b}(s,p) coincides with that of b⁡(s)b(s).

Proof: (1) Set J:=𝒥Y​(u)pJ:={\mathcal{J}}_{Y}(u)_{p}, which is an ideal of (𝒪Y)p​[s]({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s]. The existence of b~​(s,x′′)\tilde{b}(s,x^{\prime\prime}) follows from b⁡(s)∈(𝒪Y)p​[s]∩Jb(s)\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s]\cap J. Dividing b⁡(s)b(s) by b~​(s,x′′)\tilde{b}(s,x^{\prime\prime}) in (𝒪Y)p​[s]({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s], we obtain

b⁡(s)=q⁡(s,x′′)​b~​(s,x′′)+c⁡(s,x′′)b(s)=q(s,x^{\prime\prime})\tilde{b}(s,x^{\prime\prime})+c(s,x^{\prime\prime})

with q⁡(s,x′′),c⁡(s,x′′)∈(𝒪Y)p​[s]q(s,x^{\prime\prime}),c(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s] such that the degree of c⁡(s,x′′)c(s,x^{\prime\prime}) in ss is less than that of b~​(s,x′′)\tilde{b}(s,x^{\prime\prime}). By the proof of the preceding proposition, c⁡(s,p)=0c(s,p)=0 holds since c⁡(s,x′′)∈Jc(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in J.

(2) Let s1,…,sds_{1},\dots,s_{d} be the distinct zeros of b~​(s,p)\tilde{b}(s,p). Let us show that b⁡(s)b(s) has no other zeros. Suppose this is not the case and let sd+1,…,sd+ks_{d+1},\dots,s_{d+k} be the distinct zeros of b⁡(s)b(s) other than s1,…,sds_{1},\dots,s_{d}, with multiplicities m1,…,mkm_{1},\dots,m_{k}. Set

b1(s):=(s−sd+1)m1⋯(s−sd+k)mk,b0(s):=b(s)/b1(s).b_{1}(s):=(s-s_{d+1})^{m_{1}}\cdots(s-s_{d+k})^{m_{k}},\quad b_{0}(s):=b(s)/b_{1}(s).

Then b1​(s)b_{1}(s) and b~​(s,x)\tilde{b}(s,x) both belongs to the ideal

B:=J:b0​(s)={f⁡(s,x′′)∈(𝒪Y)p​[s]∣f⁡(s,x′′)​b0​(s)∈J}B:=J:b_{0}(s)=\{f(s,x^{\prime\prime})\in({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s]\mid f(s,x^{\prime\prime})b_{0}(s)\in J\}

of (𝒪Y)p​[s]({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s]. Let

r⁡(x):=Res⁡(b~​(s,x),b1​(s))r(x):=\mathrm{Res}(\tilde{b}(s,x),b_{1}(s))

be the resultant with respect to ss. Then r⁡(x)r(x) belongs to BB. Since b~​(s,x)\tilde{b}(s,x) and b1​(s)b_{1}(s) are monic in ss,

r⁡(p)=Res⁡(b~​(s,p),b1​(s))r(p)=\mathrm{Res}(\tilde{b}(s,p),b_{1}(s))

is a nonzero constant since b~​(s,p)\tilde{b}(s,p) and b1​(s)b_{1}(s) have no common zeros. This implies B=(𝒪Y)p​[s]B=({\mathcal{O}}_{Y})_{p}[s] and hence b0​(s)b_{0}(s) belongs to JJ, which is a contradiciton. □\Box

Corollary 1

If there exists an indicial polynomial of uu along YY at pp that belongs to ℂ⁡[s]{\mathbb{C}}[s], then it is the bb-function of uu at pp.

2 Indicial polynomials and bb-functions with respect to coherent ideals

We follow the method by Budur-Mustaţã-Saito [2] of defining the Bernstein-Sato polynomial for an arbitrary subvariety, possibly with multiplicities, in a slightly more general settings.

Let XX be an nn-dimensional complex manifold and let ℱ{\mathcal{F}} be a coherent sheaf of ideals of 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. Let pp be a point of the support of 𝒪X/ℱ{\mathcal{O}}_{X}/{\mathcal{F}}. Let f1,…,fdf_{1},\dots,f_{d} be a set of local generators of ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on a Stein open neighborhood UU of pp. Then fi​(p)=0f_{i}(p)=0 holds for i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d.

Consider the associated graph embedding

ι:U∋x⟼(x,f1​(x),…,fd​(x))∈U×ℂd.\iota:U\ni x\longmapsto(x,f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{d}(x))\in U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}.

Then

Z:=ι(U)={(x,t1,…,td)∈U×ℂd∣ti=fi(x)(i=1,…,d)}Z:=\iota(U)=\{(x,t_{1},\dots,t_{d})\in U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}\mid t_{i}=f_{i}(x)\quad(i=1,\dots,d)\}

is a (non-singular) closed submanifold of ℂd×U{\mathbb{C}}^{d}\times U, which depends on the choice of local generators f1,…,fdf_{1},\dots,f_{d} of ℱ{\mathcal{F}}. Let ℐZ{\mathcal{I}}_{Z} be the defining ideal of ZZ and set

Γ[Z](𝒢):={u∈𝒢∣ℐZku=0(∃k∈ℕ)}\Gamma_{[Z]}({\mathcal{G}}):=\{u\in{\mathcal{G}}\mid{\mathcal{I}}_{Z}^{k}u=0\quad(\exists k\in{\mathbb{N}})\}

for a 𝒪U×ℂd{\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}-module 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. Let ℬZ|U×ℂd:=ℋ[Z]d​(𝒪U×ℂd){\mathcal{B}}_{Z|U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}:={\mathcal{H}}^{d}_{[Z]}({\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}) be the dd-th algebraic local (or relative) cohomology group of 𝒪U×ℂd{\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}} supported by ZZ, where ℋ[Z]d{\mathcal{H}}^{d}_{[Z]} is the dd-th right derived functor of Γ[Z]\Gamma_{[Z]}. Then ℬZ|U×ℂd{\mathcal{B}}_{Z|U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}} has a natural strucuture of holonomic left 𝒟X×ℂd{\mathcal{D}}_{X\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}-module (see Kashiwara [5], [6]). Suppose that ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is a coherent left 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module defined on UU. Then the DD-module theoretic direct image of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} associated with the embedding ι\iota is the left 𝒟U×ℂd{\mathcal{D}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}-module

ι∗​(ℳ):=ℳ⊗𝒪X|UℬZ|U×ℂd.\iota_{*}({\mathcal{M}}):={\mathcal{M}}\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X}|_{U}}{\mathcal{B}}_{Z|U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}.

The functor ι∗\iota_{*} is exact and sends a coherent (resp. holonomic) 𝒟U{\mathcal{D}}_{U}-module to a coherent (resp. holonomic) 𝒟U×ℂd{\mathcal{D}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}-module.

Let uu be a section of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} defined on a neighborhood of pp. Then

ι∗(u):=u⊗δ(t1−f1)⋯δ(td−fd)\iota_{*}(u):=u\otimes\delta(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots\delta(t_{d}-f_{d})

is defined as a section of ι∗​(ℳ)\iota_{*}({\mathcal{M}}). Here δ(t1−f1)⋯δ(td−fd)\delta(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots\delta(t_{d}-f_{d}) is the residue class

[1(t1−f1)⋯(td−fd)]∈𝒪U×ℂd​[h−1]/∑j=1d𝒪U×ℂd​[hj−1]≃ℋ[Z]d​(𝒪U×ℂd)\left[\frac{1}{(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots(t_{d}-f_{d})}\right]\in{\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}[h^{-1}]/\sum_{j=1}^{d}{\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}}[h_{j}^{-1}]\simeq{\mathcal{H}}^{d}_{[Z]}({\mathcal{O}}_{U\times{\mathbb{C}}^{d}})

with h:=(t1−f1)⋯(td−fd)h:=(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots(t_{d}-f_{d}) and hj:=h/(tj−fj)h_{j}:=h/(t_{j}-f_{j}). If ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is generated by uu, then ι∗​(ℳ)\iota_{*}({\mathcal{M}}) is generated by ι∗​(u)\iota_{*}(u). See Algorithm 1 for a concrete description of ι∗​(ℳ)\iota_{*}({\mathcal{M}}) in this case. The first statement of the following theorem is due to Budur-Mustaţã-Saito [2].

Theorem 1

In the notation above

  1. 1.

    Assume that there exists the bb-function b⁡(s)b(s) of ι∗​(u)\iota_{*}(u) along U×{0}U\times\{0\} at ι⁡(p)\iota(p). Let YY be a closed analytic subset of a complex manifold XX. We denote ℐY{\mathcal{I}}_{Y} the defining ideal of YY, which is a coherent sheaf of ideals of 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. Let uu be a section of a coherent 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module ℳ{\mathcal{M}} defined on a neighborhood of a non-singular point pp of YY. Then at pp, we can relate the bb-function and an indicial polynomial of uu along YY defined in Section 1 to those of uu with respect to ℐY{\mathcal{I}}_{Y} defined in Section 2. This is crucial in actual computation.

4 Inverse image of a DD-module

In this section, we assume that XX is a (n+d)(n+d)-dimensional complex manifold and YY is a closed submanifold of XX of codimension dd. Around a given point pp of YY, we choose a local coordinate system (x,t)=(x1,…,xn,t1,…,td)(x,t)=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},t_{1},\dots,t_{d}) such that YY is defined by t1=⋯=td=0t_{1}=\dots=t_{d}=0.

Set 𝒟Y→X:=𝒪Y⊗𝒪X𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{Y\rightarrow X}:={\mathcal{O}}_{Y}\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X}}{\mathcal{D}}_{X}, which is a (𝒟Y,𝒟X)({\mathcal{D}}_{Y},{\mathcal{D}}_{X})-bimodule on YY. In the local coordinate system (x,t)(x,t), we have

𝒟Y→X≃𝒟X/(t1​𝒟X+⋯+td​𝒟X).{\mathcal{D}}_{Y\rightarrow X}\simeq{\mathcal{D}}_{X}/(t_{1}{\mathcal{D}}_{X}+\cdots+t_{d}{\mathcal{D}}_{X}).

The inverse image of a coherent 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-module ℳ{\mathcal{M}} with respect to the embedding ι:Y→X\iota:Y\rightarrow X is defined by

𝕃ι∗(ℳ):=𝒟Y→X⊗𝒟X𝕃ℳ\mathbb{L}\iota^{*}({\mathcal{M}}):={\mathcal{D}}_{Y\rightarrow X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathbb{L}}}{{\otimes}}_{{\mathcal{D}}_{X}}{\mathcal{M}}

in the derived category D−​(Mod⁡(𝒟Y))D^{-}(\mathrm{Mod}({\mathcal{D}}_{Y})) of complexes of left 𝒟Y{\mathcal{D}}_{Y}-modules bounded above (see Kashiwara [6]). It is also called the (DD-module theoretic) restriction of ℳ{\mathcal{M}} to YY.

It follows from a theorem of Laurent-Schapira [11] that if there exists an indicial polynomial along YY for each section of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, then the cohomology groups of 𝕃​ι∗​(ℳ)\mathbb{L}\iota^{*}({\mathcal{M}}) are coherent 𝒟Y{\mathcal{D}}_{Y}-modules. In the sequel let us give a concrete expression of the cohomology groups.

For an integer vector 𝐦=(m1,…,mk)∈ℤk{\bf m}=(m_{1},\dots,m_{k})\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{k}, we define the shifted VV-filtration

VYi​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k):=VYi−m1​(𝒟X)⊕⋯⊕VYi−mk​(𝒟X)V_{Y}^{i}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k}):=V_{Y}^{i-m_{1}}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{Y}^{i-m_{k}}({\mathcal{D}}_{X})

on the free module (𝒟X)k({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k}. The associaed graded module is defined by

grY​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k):=⨁i∈ℤgrYi​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k)\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k}):=\bigoplus_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{i}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k})

with

grYi​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k):=VYi​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k)/VYi−1​[𝐦]​((𝒟X)k).\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{i}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k}):=V_{Y}^{i}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k})/V_{Y}^{i-1}[{\bf m}](({\mathcal{D}}_{X})^{k}).

We omit [𝐦][{\bf m}] if 𝐦{\bf m} is the zero vector. There exists an exact sequence

of left 𝒟X{\mathcal{D}}_{X}-modules together with vectors 𝐦1∈ℤr1{\bf m}_{1}\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{r_{1}}, ..., 𝐦l∈ℤrl{\bf m}_{l}\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{r_{l}} such that

5 Algebraic formulation

Let us consider the algebraic version of bb-functions and indicial polynomials. We have only to treat bb-functions and indicial polynomials along a linear subspace by using the graph embedding.

In what follows we fix a field KK of characteristic zero, which we regard as the ‘base field’ over which all the data are defined, and an algebraic closed field Ω\Omega which contains all fields we work with. We also introduce an intermediate field LL such that K⊂L⊂ΩK\subset L\subset\Omega in order to clarify the dependence of indicial polynomials and bb-functions on the coefficient field. Most typically, we set K=ℚK={\mathbb{Q}}, Ω=ℂ\Omega={\mathbb{C}} and let LL be an algebraic extension field of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

Let X:=Kn+dX:=K^{n+d} be the (n+d)(n+d)-dimensional affine space over KK and let (x,t)=(x1,…,xn,t1,…,td)(x,t)=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},t_{1},\dots,t_{d}) be its coordinates. Let Y:=X×{0}⊂X×KdY:=X\times\{0\}\subset X\times K^{d} be the nn-dimensional affine subspace of XX with the coordinates xx.

Let us denote by DnD_{n} the ring of differential operators with polynomial coefficients in nn variables xx over KK, and by Dn+dD_{n+d} that in (n+d)(n+d)-variables (x,t)(x,t). The VV-filtration on Dn+dD_{n+d} with respect to YY is defined by

VYi(Dn+d):={P∈Dn+d∣P⟨t1,…,td⟩j⊂⟨t1,…,td)⟩j−i(∀j∈ℤ)}(i∈ℤ),V^{i}_{Y}(D_{n+d}):=\{P\in D_{n+d}\mid P\langle t_{1},\dots,t_{d}\rangle^{j}\subset\langle t_{1},\dots,t_{d})\rangle^{j-i}\quad(\forall j\in{\mathbb{Z}})\}\quad(i\in{\mathbb{Z}}),

where ⟨t1,…,td⟩\langle t_{1},\dots,t_{d}\rangle is the ideal of K⁡[t,x]K[t,x] generated by t1,…,tdt_{1},\dots,t_{d}. The associated graded ring is defined to be

grY​(Dn+d):=⨁i∈ℤgrYi​(Dn+d),grYi​(Dn+d):=VYi​(Dn+d)/VYi−1​(Dn+d).\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}(D_{n+d}):=\bigoplus_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{i}(D_{n+d}),\qquad\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{i}(D_{n+d}):=V^{i}_{Y}(D_{n+d})/V_{Y}^{i-1}(D_{n+d}).

Let MM be a finitely generated left Dn+dD_{n+d}-module and uu a nonzero element of MM. The left ideal

AnnDn+d​u:={P∈Dn+d∣P​u=0}{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u:=\{P\in D_{n+d}\mid Pu=0\}

of Dn+dD_{n+d} is called the annihilator (ideal) of uu. Then

grYi​(AnnDn+d​u):=(VYi​(Dn+d)∩AnnDn+d​u)/(VYi−1​(Dn+d)∩AnnDn+d​u)(i∈ℤ)\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{i}_{Y}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u):=(V^{i}_{Y}(D_{n+d})\cap{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)/(V^{i-1}_{Y}(D_{n+d})\cap{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\qquad(i\in{\mathbb{Z}})

is a left grY0​(Dn+d)\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{0}(D_{n+d})-submodule of grYi​(Dn+d)\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{i}_{Y}(D_{n+d}). The residue class of P∈VYi​(Dn+d)P\in V_{Y}^{i}(D_{n+d}) belongs to grYi​(AnnDn+d​u)\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{i}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u) if and only if there exists Q∈VYi−1​(Dn+d)Q\in V_{Y}^{i-1}(D_{n+d}) such that (P+Q)​u=0(P+Q)u=0. Set θ:=t1∂t1+⋯+td∂td\theta:=t_{1}\partial_{t_{1}}+\cdots+t_{d}\partial_{t_{d}} and let ss be the residue class of θ\theta in grY0​(Dn+d)\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{0}(D_{n+d}). Then grY0​(AnnDn+d​u)∩K⁡[s,x]\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{0}_{Y}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\cap K[s,x] is an ideal of the polynomial ring K⁡[s,x]K[s,x]. We define an ideal JY​(u)J_{Y}(u) of K⁡[s,x]K[s,x] by

JY​(u):=grY0​(AnnDn+d​u)∩K⁡[s,x].J_{Y}(u):=\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{0}_{Y}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\cap K[s,x].

We remark that

L⊗KJY​(u)=L⊗KgrY0​(AnnDn+d​u)∩L⁡[s,x]=grY0​(L⊗KAnnDn+d​u)∩L⁡[s,x]L\otimes_{K}J_{Y}(u)=L\otimes_{K}\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{0}_{Y}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\cap L[s,x]=\mbox{{\rm gr}}^{0}_{Y}(L\otimes_{K}{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\cap L[s,x]

holds for any extension field LL of KK.

Definition 3

Let p=(c1,…,cn)p=(c_{1},\dots,c_{n}) be a point of Ωn\Omega^{n} and LL a subfield of Ω\Omega. Then we set

ZL​(p):={f⁡(x)∈L⁡[x]∣f⁡(p)=0},Z_{L}(p):=\{f(x)\in L[x]\mid f(p)=0\},

which is a prime ideal of L⁡[x]L[x]. In particular, ZΩ​(p)Z_{\Omega}(p) is the maximal ideal of Ω⁡[x]\Omega[x] generated by x1−c1,…,xn−cnx_{1}-c_{1},\dots,x_{n}-c_{n}, and ZL​(p)=ZΩ​(p)∩L⁡[x]Z_{L}(p)=Z_{\Omega}(p)\cap L[x].

For example, set Ω=ℂ\Omega={\mathbb{C}} and p=(α,α​2)∈ℂ2p=(\alpha,\alpha\sqrt{2})\in{\mathbb{C}}^{2} with a transcendental number α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}. Then we have

Zℚ​(p)=⟨2​x12−x22⟩,Zℚ⁡(2)​(p)=⟨2​x1−x2⟩,Zℂ​(p)=⟨x1−α,x2−2​α⟩.Z_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(p)=\langle 2x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2}\rangle,\quad Z_{{\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{2})}(p)=\langle\sqrt{2}x_{1}-x_{2}\rangle,\quad Z_{{\mathbb{C}}}(p)=\langle x_{1}-\alpha,x_{2}-\sqrt{2}\alpha\rangle.

It is natural to specify a point pp of Ωn\Omega^{n} in terms of the ideal ZL​(p)Z_{L}(p) rather than the coordinates of pp. In fact, for any algebraic extension LL of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} and any prime ideal 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} of L⁡[x]L[x], there exists a point pp of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} such that 𝔭=ZL​(p){\mathfrak{p}}=Z_{L}(p); see Proposition 1.4 of [13]. That is, the map ℂn∋p↦ZL​(p)∈Spec​L​[x]{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\ni p\mapsto Z_{L}(p)\in\mathrm{Spec}\,L[x] is surjective. We shall see that an indicial polynomial at pp is determined by the ideal ZL​(p)Z_{L}(p). However, we need a condition on LL for the bb-function at pp to be determined by ZL​(p)Z_{L}(p), in general.

Definition 4

Let MM, uu be as above and LL be an extension field of KK. Let 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} be a prime ideal of L⁡[x]L[x]. Set JY(u)𝔭:=L[x]𝔭⊗L⁡[x]L⊗KJY(u)J_{Y}(u)_{\mathfrak{p}}:=L[x]_{\mathfrak{p}}\otimes_{L[x]}L\otimes_{K}J_{Y}(u), which is an ideal of L​[x]𝔭​[s]L[x]_{\mathfrak{p}}[s]; here L​[x]𝔭L[x]_{\mathfrak{p}} denotes the localization of L⁡[x]L[x] with respect to the multiplicative set L⁡[x]∖𝔭L[x]\setminus{\mathfrak{p}}. Then the monic generator of the ideal JY​(u)𝔭∩L⁡[s]J_{Y}(u)_{\mathfrak{p}}\cap L[s] of L⁡[s]L[s], if it is not {0}\{0\}, is called the bb-function of uu along YY at the prime ideal 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}}, which we denote by b𝔭​(s)b_{\mathfrak{p}}(s). The monic generator of the ideal JY​(u)∩K​[s]J_{Y}(u)\cap K[s], if it is not {0}\{0\}, is called the global bb-function of uu along YY.

The condition b𝔭​(s)∈JY​(u)𝔭b_{\mathfrak{p}}(s)\in J_{Y}(u)_{\mathfrak{p}} is equivalent to the existence of a⁡(x)∈L⁡[x]∖𝔭a(x)\in L[x]\setminus{\mathfrak{p}} such that a⁡(x)​b𝔭​(s)∈L⊗KJY​(u)a(x)b_{\mathfrak{p}}(s)\in L\otimes_{K}J_{Y}(u). The correspondence 𝔭↦b𝔭​(s){\mathfrak{p}}\mapsto b_{\mathfrak{p}}(s) defines a map Spec ​L​[x]→L⁡[s]\mbox{{\rm Spec}\,}L[x]\rightarrow L[s]. If 𝔭1{\mathfrak{p}}_{1} and 𝔭2{\mathfrak{p}}_{2} are prime ideals of L⁡[x]L[x] with 𝔭1⊂𝔭2{\mathfrak{p}}_{1}\subset{\mathfrak{p}}_{2}, then b𝔭1​(s)b_{{\mathfrak{p}}_{1}}(s) divides b𝔭2​(s)b_{{\mathfrak{p}}_{2}}(s) since L​[x]𝔭2⊂L​[x]𝔭1L[x]_{{\mathfrak{p}}_{2}}\subset L[x]_{{\mathfrak{p}}_{1}}. The following fact is well-known for the classical Bernstein-Sato polynomial.

Proposition 3

Let LL be an arbitrary extension field of KK. The global bb-function b⁡(s)∈K⁡[x]b(s)\in K[x] of uu along YY is the least common multiple of the bb-functions of uu at the maximal ideals of L⁡[x]L[x]. In particular, the global bb-function exists if and only if the bb-function at every maximal ideal of L⁡[x]L[x] exists.

which is a proper ideal of L⁡[x]L[x] by the assumption. Let 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} be a maximal ideal of L⁡[x]L[x] which contains II. There exists a⁡(x)∈L⁡[x]∖𝔭a(x)\in L[x]\setminus{\mathfrak{p}} such that a⁡(x)​b𝔭​(s)∈L⊗KJY​(u)a(x)b_{\mathfrak{p}}(s)\in L\otimes_{K}J_{Y}(u). The bb-function essentially depends on the field extension LL of KK in general.

Proposition 4

Proof: Let us define a filtration of L⁡[s,x]L[s,x] by

The proof is almost the same as that of Theorem 1. However, an algebraic formulation of Theorem 2 is not straightforward; one needs to algebraically flatten out the algebraic variety YY, which is not always possible, or to work with DD-modules on YY directly. Nevertheless, it does not cause any problem concerning the computation of indicial polynomials and bb-functions along YY in the analytic sense via algebraic graph embedding as in Theorem 3, as will be certified in the next section.

7 Algorithms

7.1 Computation of the graph embedding

Let X:=KnX:=K^{n} be the nn-dimensional affine space over a field KK of characteristic 00 and let x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) be its coordinates. Let us denote by DnD_{n} the ring of differential operators with polynomial coefficients in nn variables xx over KK. Let t=(t1,…,td)t=(t_{1},\dots,t_{d}) be the coordinates of the affine space KdK^{d}. We denote Dn+dD_{n+d} the ring of differential operators in (n+d)(n+d)-variables (x,t)(x,t).

Let f1,…,fdf_{1},\dots,f_{d} be polynomials in K⁡[x]K[x] and let ι\iota be the embedding defined by

ι:Kn∋x⟼(x,f1​(x),…,fd​(x))∈Kn×Kd.\iota\,:\,K^{n}\ni x\longmapsto(x,f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{d}(x))\in K^{n}\times K^{d}.

For a DD-module M=D​uM=Du, the direct image ι∗​(M)\iota_{*}(M) can be computed by the following algorithm, which is essentially due to Walther [22].

Algorithm 1

Input: A set GG of generators of the left ideal AnnDn​u{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n}}u of DnD_{n}.
Output: A set G′G^{\prime} of generators of the left ideal AnnDn+d​ι∗​(u){\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}\iota_{*}(u) of Dn+dD_{n+d}.

  1. 1.

    For P=P(x,∂x1,…,∂xn)∈GP=P(x,\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{n}})\in G, set

    τ(P,f1,…,fd):=P(x,∂x1+∑j=1d∂fj∂x1∂tj,…,∂xn+∑j=1d∂fj∂xn∂tj).\tau(P,f_{1},\dots,f_{d}):=P\left(x,\,\partial_{x_{1}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial{x_{1}}}\partial_{t_{j}},\dots,\partial_{x_{n}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial{x_{n}}}\partial_{t_{j}}\right).

    This substitution is well-defined in the ring Dn+dD_{n+d} since the operators which are substituted for ∂x1,…,∂xn\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{n}} commute with one another.

  2. 2.

    Set

    G′:={τ(P,f1,…,fd)∣P∈G}∪{tj−fj(x)∣j=1,…,d}.G^{\prime}:=\{\tau(P,f_{1},\dots,f_{d})\mid P\in G\}\cup\{t_{j}-f_{j}(x)\mid j=1,\dots,d\}.

(∂xi+∑j=1d∂fj∂xi∂tj)ι∗(u)\displaystyle\left(\partial_{x_{i}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}\partial_{t_{j}}\right)\iota_{*}(u) =(∂xi+∑j=1d∂fj∂xi∂tj)(u⊗δ(t1−f1)⋯δ(td−fd))\displaystyle=\left(\partial_{x_{i}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}\partial_{t_{j}}\right)(u\otimes\delta(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots\delta(t_{d}-f_{d}))
=(∂xiu)⊗δ(t1−f1)⋯δ(td−fd).\displaystyle=(\partial_{x_{i}}u)\otimes\delta(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots\delta(t_{d}-f_{d}).

Conversely, suppose that P∈Dn+pP\in D_{n+p} annihilates ι∗​(u)\iota_{*}(u). We can rewrite PP in the form

P=∑α∈ℕn,ν∈ℕdpα,ν(x)∂tν(∂x1+∑j=1d∂fj∂x1∂tj)α1⋯(∂xn+∑j=1d∂fj∂xn∂tj)αn+∑j=1dQj⋅(tj−fj(x))P=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n},\nu\in{\mathbb{N}}^{d}}p_{\alpha,\nu}(x)\partial_{t}^{\nu}\Bigl(\partial_{x_{1}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial{x_{1}}}\partial_{t_{j}}\Bigr)^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\Bigl(\partial_{x_{n}}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial{x_{n}}}\partial_{t_{j}}\Bigr)^{\alpha_{n}}\\ +\sum_{j=1}^{d}Q_{j}\cdot(t_{j}-f_{j}(x))

with pα,ν​(x)∈K​[x]p_{\alpha,\nu}(x)\in K[x] and Qj∈Dn+pQ_{j}\in D_{n+p}. Setting Pν:=∑α∈ℕnpα,ν(x)∂xαP_{\nu}:=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}}p_{\alpha,\nu}(x)\partial_{x}^{\alpha}, we get

=∑ν∈ℕdPνu⊗∂tνδ(t1−f1)⋯δ(td−fd).\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu\in{\mathbb{N}}^{d}}P_{\nu}u\otimes\partial_{t}^{\nu}\delta(t_{1}-f_{1})\cdots\delta(t_{d}-f_{d}).

P=∑ν∈ℕd∂tντ⁡(Pν,f1,…,fd)+∑j=1dQj⋅(tj−fj​(x))∈J.P=\sum_{\nu\in{\mathbb{N}}^{d}}\partial_{t}^{\nu}\tau(P_{\nu},f_{1},\dots,f_{d})+\sum_{j=1}^{d}Q_{j}\cdot(t_{j}-f_{j}(x))\,\,\in J.

7.2 Computation of an indicial polynomial

Following the notation in Section 5, let X:=Kn+dX:=K^{n+d} be the (n+d)(n+d)-dimensional affine space over KK and let (x,t)=(x1,…,xn,t1,…,td)(x,t)=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},t_{1},\dots,t_{d}) be its coordinates. Let Y:=X×{0}⊂X×KdY:=X\times\{0\}\subset X\times K^{d} be the nn-dimensional affine subspace of XX with the coordinates xx.

Let us denote by DnD_{n} the ring of differential operators with polynomial coefficients in nn variables xx over KK, and by Dn+dD_{n+d} that in (n+d)(n+d)-variables (x,t)(x,t).

First let us give an algorithm for computing algebraic indicial polynomials. Let KK be the base field, most typically ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, over which the data are defined. Let uu be a nonzero element of a finitely generated Dn+dD_{n+d}-module MM as in Section 5. First we compute the ideal JY​(u):=K⁡[s,x]∩grY​(AnnDn+d​u)J_{Y}(u):=K[s,x]\cap\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u) by the first two steps of Algorithm 4.6 of [19]. An outline of the algorithm is as follows:

Algorithm 2

Input: a set of generators of the left ideal AnnDn+d​u{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u of Dn+dD_{n+d}.
Output: a set of generators of the ideal JY​(u)J_{Y}(u) of K⁡[s,x]K[s,x].

  1. 1.

    Compute a Gröbner basis of AnnDn+d​u{\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n}+d}u which is adapted to the VYV_{Y}-filtration and extract a set of generators of grY0​(AnnDn+d​u)\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{0}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u).

  2. 2.

    Compute the intersection I:=grY0(AnnDn+du)∩K[t1∂t1,…,td∂td]⊗KDnI:=\mbox{{\rm gr}}_{Y}^{0}({\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u)\cap K[t_{1}\partial_{t_{1}},\dots,t_{d}\partial_{t_{d}}]\otimes_{K}D_{n} by using multi-homogenization with respect to the pairs (t1,∂t1),…,(td,∂td)(t_{1},\partial_{t_{1}}),\dots,(t_{d},\partial_{t_{d}}).

  3. 3.

    Compute the intersection JY​(u)=I∩K⁡[θ,x]J_{Y}(u)=I\cap K[\theta,x] by elimination.

Now that a set of generators of JY​(u)J_{Y}(u) is obtained, the rest of the computations are done in polynomial rings.

Algorithm 3

Input: a set of generators of the ideal JY​(u)J_{Y}(u) of K⁡[s,x]K[s,x] and a set of generators of a prime ideal 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} of K⁡[x]K[x].
Output: an indicial polynomial b⁡(s,x)∈K​[x]𝔭​[s]b(s,x)\in K[x]_{\mathfrak{p}}[s] of uu along YY at 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} of K⁡[x]K[x] if there is one.

  1. 1.

    Compute a reduced Gröbner basis G={f1,…,fm}G=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\} of JY​(u)J_{Y}(u) with respect to a term order ≺\prec such that x1,…,xn≺sx_{1},\dots,x_{n}\prec s. Let ai∈K⁡[x]a_{i}\in K[x] be the leading coefficient of fif_{i} with respect to ss.

  2. 2.

    Set N:=max{degsfi∣i=1,…,m}N:=\max\{\deg_{s}f_{i}\mid i=1,\dots,m\}. For each k=0,…,Nk=0,\dots,N, let IkI_{k} be the ideal of K⁡[x]K[x] generated by {ai∣degs⁡fi≤k⁡(i=1,…,m)}\{a_{i}\mid\deg_{s}f_{i}\leq k\,(i=1,\dots,m)\}.

  3. 3.

    If IN⊄𝔭I_{N}\not\subset{\mathfrak{p}}, set k0:=min⁡{k∣Ik⊄𝔭}k_{0}:=\min\{k\mid I_{k}\not\subset{\mathfrak{p}}\}. Then there exists fi∈Gf_{i}\in G such that degs⁡fi=k\deg_{s}f_{i}=k and ai∉𝔭a_{i}\not\in{\mathfrak{p}}. Set b⁡(s,x):=fi​(s,x)/ai​(x)b(s,x):=f_{i}(s,x)/a_{i}(x). If IN⊂𝔭I_{N}\subset{\mathfrak{p}}, then there is no indicial polynomial at 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}}.

If KK is a subfield of ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, this algorithm provides a stratification of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with respect to the degree of indicial polynomials. In the notation of the preceding algorithm, set

Vk:=𝕍⁡(Ik)={p∈ℂn∣a⁡(p)=0 for any a∈Ik}.V_{k}:=\mathbb{V}(I_{k})=\{p\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\mid\mbox{$a(p)=0$ for any $a\in I_{k}$}\}.

Then VkV_{k} is a decreasing sequence of alebraic sets of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. An indicial polynomial at the maximal ideal Zℂ​(p)Z_{\mathbb{C}}(p) exists and its degree is kk for any p∈Vk−1∖Vkp\in V_{k-1}\setminus V_{k} with k=0,1,…,Nk=0,1,\dots,N; here we set V−1=ℂnV_{-1}={\mathbb{C}}^{n}. Moreover, if we choose fi∈Gf_{i}\in G such that degs⁡fi=k\deg_{s}f_{i}=k, then fi/aif_{i}/a_{i} is an indicial polynomial at Zℂ​(p)Z_{\mathbb{C}}(p) for any p∈Vk−1∖Vkp\in V_{k-1}\setminus V_{k} such that ai​(p)≠0a_{i}(p)\neq 0. Note that we do not need field extension in the computations above.

7.3 Computation of the bb-function

Let us review existing algorithms for computing bb-functions. First in [17], an algorithm (Algorithm 4.5) to compute the bb-function of a DD-module along a hyperplane at a point of KnK^{n} was given. This algorithm is based on the fact that the roots of the bb-function at a point pp coincides with the zeros of the ideal JY​(u)​(K¯)|x=pJ_{Y}(u)(\overline{K})|_{x=p} of K¯​[s]\overline{K}[s] (Thoerem 4.6 of [17]), which also follows from Propositions 1 and 2 in Section 1 and does not require the (existence of) global bb-function. However, it requires factorization of a univariate polynomial into linear factors in general, which in fact is unnecessary for the classical Bernstein-Sato polynomial by virtue of Kashiwara’s theorem [4].

Secondly, an algorithm for computing bb-functions of a DD-module along an affine subspace of arbitrary codimension with a corresponding stratification was proposed in [19] (Algorithm 4.6). This algorithm makes use of a primary decomposition of the ideal L⊗KJY​(u)L\otimes_{K}J_{Y}(u) for a stratification. In order to compute the bb-function at a point, one can use the method of [17] mentioned above. Note also that the algorithm in [19] can be readily applied to the computation of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of an arbitrary variety in the sense of Budur-Mustaţã-Saito [2]; in fact, Example 4.7 in [19] is the computation of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of the variety defined by the ideal ⟨x3−y2,y3−z2⟩\langle x^{3}-y^{2},y^{3}-z^{2}\rangle.

Thirdly, Nishiyama and Noro [14] introduced a much more efficient algorithm to compute a stratification with respect to the Bernstein-Sato polynomial without primary decomposition. In fact, their method also applies to the bb-function of a DD-module if the global bb-function exists and its factorization into linear factors in the splitting field is obtained.

Our algorithm for indicial polynomials provides a heuristic method for computing the bb-function with an associated stratification without field extension, the global bb-function, or primary decomposition, especially for holonomic DD-modules including the case with Bernstein-Sato polynomials (see Example 11 below).

7.4 Case with parameters

Let y=(y1,…,ym)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{m}) be indeterminates and M=Dn+d​[y]​uM=D_{n+d}[y]u be a Dn+d​[y]D_{n+d}[y]-module generated by u∈Mu\in M. Once an indicial polynomial b⁡(s,x)b(s,x) of uu along YY at a prime ideal 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} of K⁡[x]K[x] is obtained, it is also important to find a differential operator PP which belongs to K​[x]𝔭⊗K⁡[x]VY−1​(Dn+d)K[x]_{\mathfrak{p}}\otimes_{K[x]}V_{Y}^{-1}(D_{n+d}) and satisfies

Let ≺\prec be an ordering for the monomials in Dn+dD_{n+d} which is compatible with the filtration {VYj​(Dn+d)}\{V_{Y}^{j}(D_{n+d})\} and induces a well-ordering among the monomials in VYj​(Dn+d)∖VYj−1​(Dn+d)V_{Y}^{j}(D_{n+d})\setminus V_{Y}^{j-1}(D_{n+d}) for each jj. Let P1,…,PkP_{1},\dots,P_{k} be a Gröbner basis of I:=AnnDn+d​uI:={\mathrm{Ann}}_{D_{n+d}}u with respect to ≺\prec, which can be computed by the Buchberger algorithm with homogenization although ≺\prec is not a well-ordering (see [17], [19]). There exists a⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]∖𝔭a(x)\in K[x]\setminus{\mathfrak{p}} such that a⁡(x)​b​(s,x)∈JY​(u)a(x)b(s,x)\in J_{Y}(u). By the (partial) division algorithm, we can find Q1,…,Qk,R∈Dn+dQ_{1},\dots,Q_{k},R\in D_{n+d} such that

a⁡(x)​b​(θ,x)=Q1​P1+⋯+Qk​Pk+Ra(x)b(\theta,x)=Q_{1}P_{1}+\cdots+Q_{k}P_{k}+R

with Qi​Pi∈VY0​(Dn+d)Q_{i}P_{i}\in V_{Y}^{0}(D_{n+d}), R∈VY−1​(Dn+d)R\in V_{Y}^{-1}(D_{n+d}). Then (a⁡(x)​b​(θ,x)−R)​u=0(a(x)b(\theta,x)-R)u=0 holds. Hence we can put P=−R/aP=-R/a in (7.1).

However, to find such PP of the smallest possible order is essential to the study of the solutions of the system of differential equations corresponding to uu. In particular, the system is called (weakly) regular or Fuchsian along YY if we can take such PP of order less than or equal to the degree of b⁡(s,x′′)b(s,x^{\prime\prime}) in ss. Even in this case, it is not reasonable to assume b⁡(s,x)b(s,x) is an indicial polynomial, that is, a monomic polynomial in JY​(u)𝔭⊂K​[x]𝔭​[s]J_{Y}(u)_{\mathfrak{p}}\subset K[x]_{\mathfrak{p}}[s] of the smallest degree.
